catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q1.explanation: B - whileThere is an opposition in this sentence so while is the only option.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q2.explanation: D - absoluteRelative and absolute are antonyms.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q3.explanation: D - mastersC and D are both valid collocations, but the context suggests that the person doesn’t simply get a new skill, they reach a high level of it, therefore we use verb “to master”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q4.explanation: A - after allB and C do not fit the context — they need a second part of the sentence for the opposing argument. D doesn’t fit because of punctuation — “apart from” cannot be followed by comma in this example.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q5.explanation: B - privatePrivate life is a common collocation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q6.explanation: C - spaceAgain, personal space is a collocation that means “physical space that surrounds someone”. E.g. if a stranger stands right next to you, he is within your personal space so it would be natural for you to feel uncomfortable.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q7.explanation: D - lastsIf something lasts it means that it continues for a limited amount of time, just like the context suggests.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-1-q8.explanation: C - althoughA — despite would need “that” here, B — even can’t be used without “if” in this case and D — however can’t be placed next to “but”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q9.explanation: beA passive voice has to be used here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q10.explanation: toIf something is exposed to something, it means that it is open or in contact with it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q11.explanation: some/othersThere is a clear opposition with ‘certain’ in the beginning of the sentence. In other words, one group of allergies behaves differently than the other.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q12.explanation: thatWe talk about the possibility of such allergies happening throughout the year with some good choice of modal verbs.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q13.explanation: with‘To come into contact with’ is pretty close in meaning to ‘to be exposed to’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q14.explanation: mostThe implication here is that allergies usually appear at an early age.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q15.explanation: soThe meaning of the phrase is that the symptoms can be very hard to see.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-2-q16.explanation: goes‘Come and go’ is a set phrase that means ‘to appear and later disappear again’

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q17.explanation: controversialAn adjective is required here. Controversial means that there are several opinions on it, there is a disagreement about it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q18.explanation: immortalised/immortalizedWe need a verb in past tense after “was”. To immortalise here means to give fame and eternal life through works of literature.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q19.explanation: debatableThis and the next word both should be adjectives according to their immediate contexts. Debatable means “open to discussion, doubtful”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q20.explanation: indisputableThe text states that it’s a fact therefore it shouldn’t be disputed. This clears the confusion with the previous word.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q21.explanation: remainsRemains is a plural noun which means dead body or skeleton.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q22.explanation: analysisAnalysis, not analysing (because there is an “of”preposition after the word).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-3-q23.explanation: identificationKeep in mind that you can’t use the original word without changing it, even though it would fit in this case.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q25.explanation: has gone off“To go off” (when talking of food) means to become no longer edible, e.g. get spoiled.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q26.explanation: discovery that/which the archaeologists madeDiscover = make a discovery. Make sure you spell archaeologists right.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q27.answer: would/might expect people to be less
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q27.explanation: would/might expect people to be lessWe have to use the opposite of “more” here, so it means that less has to be right before “interested”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q28.explanation: quite impossible to imagineQuite here means “somewhat”. See article about intensifiers for clarification.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q29.answer: to turn it into a profitable
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q29.explanation: to turn it into a profitableProfitable one refers to the company in question. To turn into means to make, to change.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-4-q30.explanation: was bitterly disappointed byBitterly disappointed is the only collocation that fits here. Don’t forget that “disappointed” is used with “by”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-5-q31.explanation: CSpriggs the Labrador makes the author feel at ease — he relaxes and no longer feels afraid. A and B are not mentioned, D is about dog that approaches the end of its training.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-5-q32.explanation: D“The owners have to take over … they will get out of the partnership what they put in”. Other answers are either not touched upon or mention a minor detail.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-5-q33.explanation: BMiddle of the paragraph: “… smallest piece of advice … would make a huge difference to their lives”. A is not mentioned, the word independent refers to kind of help people are getting. C isn’t mentioned; D states the opposite : “a broken wrist led him to shadow the organisation’s rehab workers”. Undeterred here means “untroubled, unhindered by”. In the reality the author was forced to change his occupation due to their trauma.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-5-q34.explanation: BAt the beginning of the paragraph it is stated that there are “many myths” surrounding the guide dogs’ job. It is after that they give a ludicrous example of fish and chips shop to illustrate how things really work.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-5-q35.explanation: CThe beginning of next paragraph “… how big a jump it is” from trusting your own eyesight to relying on dog’s guidance. B is not mentioned — it takes time to get used to the dog, nothing about controlling it. D mentioned, however it is a minor detail.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-5-q36.explanation: BThe ending of the last paragraph summarises the experience the author has had. He can relate to the extent of joy and satisfaction that the dog trainer has. A and C aren’t mentioned. D is implied by the joke made by Evans.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-6-q37.explanation: CBoth speakers are upset with the fact that people see psychologists as doctors who primarily treat mental illnesses, whereas their main aim is different. Khan: “… sports psychology is something for treating athletes with mental disorders”. Rossweller: “… most people know someone who sees a clinical psychologist or therapist for a mind-related problem.”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-6-q38.explanation: DThe second part of Khan’s paragraph is about how psychological guidance of some coaches can lead to negative outcome. Xiu Li believes that some trainers however are very capable of providing sound psychological guidance for their athletes.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-6-q39.explanation: ARemember that media involves both TV, journalism and many others. Rossweller talks about positive representation of sport psychologists on TV. Common suggests that journalists are “yet to be fully convinced” which means that journalists have their doubts about the importance of sports psychology.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-6-q40.explanation: AExpert A believes that the research needs more sophistication and better methods — implying that the current approach could be improved upon. Both experts B and C explicitly say current research is rigorous and is based on evidence, without any need for further improvement. Expert D does not criticize methods, also mentioning that the research base is significant.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-7-q41.explanation: GThe paragraph talks about the light bulb effect being “literally true”, as some parts of our brains activate whenever we get a bright idea. The next paragraph talks about blending science and culture — a reference from old cartoons are examples from lives of famous scientists from paragraph G.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-7-q42.explanation: E“All of which is not bad …” of course refers to the honorary titles mentioned before.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-7-q43.explanation: B“But no matter” discards his own acknowledgement of being a bad scientists to continue the narrative. The second part of paragraph B mentions how he got interested in Proust’s writing, and the beginning of next paragraph states that this was the start of his writing career.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-7-q44.explanation: FThe end of previous paragraph concentrates on his life in the UK, and paragraph F continues this narration.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-7-q45.explanation: CThis paragraph continues the narrative about his childhood, where he comes up with examples from his past. The second part of paragraph C introduces his latest book, How We Decide.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-7-q46.explanation: AFinally, he mentions his third book called Imagine which continues his series of books on science and, this time, art.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q47.explanation: BThe second part of the review states that “Red Riding: 1974 is the weakest of the three Red Riding films …”. The first reviewer talks about their favourite movie, not their least favourite.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q48.explanation: BThird sentence of the review states that a short toilet break is likely to make you lose the stream of narrative.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q49.explanation: DSecond part of the paragraph, starting with “The film can be too self-serious…” and how film’s “television roots show on a production level”. Reviewer C talks about production, but he admires rather than criticises it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q50.explanation: AThe second part of the paragraph states that murders aren’t the key of the film, but rather the reactions to them.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q51.explanation: CFirst sentence of the paragraph. Venue is a place where show such as movie is shown. In this case, it’s the art’s centre that chose to broadcast the movies for three weeks.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q52.explanation: DLast part of the first sentence: “… these are not sunny days for the faint of heart.” meaning that the softer viewers might find the content of the movie shocking or even revolting.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q53.explanation: DThe last sentence mentions that the film, among other things, is “expertly performed” — meaning that the actors did a good job.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q54.explanation: CLast sentence goes: “… it’s easy to forget it and its sister films were produced for British television …”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q55.explanation: BThird sentence talks about viewers from America who could be having difficulties making out the peculiar accents.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test10-part-8-q56.explanation: AThe first sentence refers to reporter Dunford as having mix of feelings.
